title: BRICKSTORM Backdoor Investigation
description: Investigate the BRICKSTORM backdoor malware compromise on the target system.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The target system has been compromised by the BRICKSTORM backdoor malware. Your task is to investigate the compromise, identify indicators of compromise (IOCs), and contain the threat. This scenario will guide you through the process of identifying suspicious services, analyzing network connections, and implementing firewall rules to mitigate the threat.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have SSH access to the target system with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. The target system's IP address is `192.168.50.5`.
levels.local_content: You have SSH access to the target system with the username `cyrano` and password `cyrano`. The target system's IP address is `192.168.50.5`.

levels.title: Identify and investigate the suspicious service running on the target system
levels.content: The target system is running a suspicious service that might be related to the BRICKSTORM backdoor. Investigate the service and identify its name. The flag is the name of the suspicious service.
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious service, you can use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services. Look for any unfamiliar or suspicious service names. The flag is the name of the suspicious service.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Check the running services on the target system to identify any unfamiliar or suspicious service names.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the `systemctl list-units --type=service` command to list all running services.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Look for the service named `vami.service` which is the suspicious service.

levels.title: Identify and investigate the suspicious outbound IP address
levels.content: The BRICKSTORM backdoor communicates with a command and control (C2) server. Identify the suspicious outbound IP address that the backdoor is communicating with. The flag is the C2 IP address.
levels.solution: To identify the suspicious outbound IP address, you can use the `ss -tulnp` command to list all network connections. Look for any unfamiliar or suspicious IP addresses. The flag is the C2 IP address in the sandbox.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Check the network connections on the target system to identify any unfamiliar or suspicious IP addresses.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the `ss -tulnp` command to list all network connections.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Look for the IP address `192.168.40.5` which is the suspicious outbound IP address.

levels.title: Contain the C2 communication
levels.content: To prevent further communication with the C2 server, you need to block the outbound connection to the identified C2 IP address and port. The flag is the port number used for C2 communication.
levels.solution: To block the outbound connection, you can use the `iptables` command to add a firewall rule. For example, `iptables -A OUTPUT -d 192.168.40.5 -j DROP` will block all outbound connections to the C2 IP address. The flag is the port number used for C2 communication.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Use firewall rules to block the outbound connection to the C2 server.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use the `iptables` command to add a firewall rule that blocks outbound connections to the C2 IP address.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The command to block the outbound connection is `iptables -A OUTPUT -d 192.168.40.5 -j DROP`.
